podcast.title: Nearly Complete Album Stolen; Band Started Over, Created American Idiot
podcast.body: By 2002, Green Day's career had stalled; their last proper album was years behind them. They recorded a follow-up called *Cigarettes and Valentines* that was almost finished when the master tapes disappeared — apparently stolen by persons unknown. Singer Billie Joe Armstrong insisted the album contained strong material; bassist Mike Dirnt acknowledged backup tapes existed but said they were inferior. The band started over entirely, creating *American Idiot*, which sold in the hundreds of millions and relaunched their career. The stolen album has never surfaced online or in bootleg form. Further suspicion: in September 2003, a mystery group called The Network released a record on Adeline Records — a label owned by Armstrong — featuring a middle section strikingly similar to an early Armstrong demo. Their identities were concealed with disguises and they staged mock feuds with Green Day. "Was there a Cigarettes and Valentines album or was it and the whole Network thing just a big joke?"

podcast.body: Around 2000, Green Day, facing career doubts, began working on an album titled "Cigarettes and Valentines," aiming for a back-to-basics sound with short, fast songs reminiscent of their pre-"Dookie" era. The sessions were successful, and the band was pleased, with a track listing and artwork prepared, until all master recordings mysteriously vanished from the studio in 2003, leading to its abandonment. "The songs were short and fast, much like what the band was doing before the dukey album more than 10 years earlier. The sessions went well and Green Day was pleased with how things were turning out. They were going to call this album, cigarettes and valentines and they were pumped about it. A track listing and some artwork were ready."

podcast.body: In 2002, after spending most of the year developing new material and completing approximately 20 songs, the master tapes for this album mysteriously vanished. The circumstances of their disappearance remain unknown and undisclosed, resulting in this project being forever known as "the lost Green Day album." This event forced the band to start their next album from scratch. "Most of 2002 was spent working on new material. They had about 20 songs done and then something weird happened. The master tapes vanished."

srcs.episode: Green Day: From their Beginning to 2005

podcast.body: In 2003, Green Day was working on a follow-up to *Warning*, creating punk-pop songs in the spirit of *Dookie*. The album, consisting of 20 songs, was allegedly stolen from the studio when it was "on the verge of being mixed." Skeptics suggest the band intentionally scrapped the album, finding it "not good enough," leading to the highly successful *American Idiot*. "It was typical Green Day stuff, fast, catchy, punk pop songs, more in the spirit of Duckey than anything they had done in the last couple of years. And things were going well too. In fact, the album was almost done when one day the band walked into the studio to find that the record had disappeared. Gone, vanished, 20 songs, poof."
